project_summary: A comparison workspace connecting Figma, Storybook and the real website, with saved visual evidence and a practical path towards release checks.
project_intro:
A component can look correct in a design file and still change when it reaches a real page. Different content, fonts, spacing or surrounding styles can make a small implementation decision visible. I built a visual testing dashboard to put those differences in one place.

The project connects three views of the same interface: the intended design in Figma, the isolated component in Storybook and its implementation on the website. It is part of how I am developing a more traceable design-to-release process.

Explore the public visual testing dashboard

story_sections.story_html:
Three sources, one review

Figma describes what I intend to build. Storybook makes a component easier to inspect away from the rest of the page. The website shows what happens when that component meets real content and the Drupal theme. Each source answers a different question, so the dashboard keeps them together.

A reviewer can open the original sources, inspect saved PNGs and use the available live previews. Missing references remain visible as missing references. Attaching a source is useful preparation, but it is not proof that the implementation matches it.

The layout can switch from three columns to stacked rows. Small controls benefit from being side by side; a navigation bar needs the width of the page. This keeps the comparison useful for both individual components and larger interface sections.

Capture the component where it actually lives

In the local dashboard, I provide a Storybook URL and a selector for the component, then add website URLs and selectors for the corresponding real examples. A selector identifies the exact element to capture; it must resolve to one element rather than an ambiguous collection.

The browser capture runs against the actual page. It waits for the relevant assets and clips the selected region, preserving the context in which the component renders. Viewport width and height are explicit settings, with presets and numeric inputs for precise values.

Valid changes to the capture settings trigger a new capture after a short pause. The current everyday workflow captures the default UI state. Hover, focus and other interaction states need deliberate coverage; they should not be assumed to have been tested just because a normal-state PNG exists.

A useful difference needs an explanation

Matching every pixel is only meaningful when the compared images have equivalent content, language, state and bounds. A longer button label should not automatically turn a useful component comparison into a failure.

The dashboard therefore uses an appearance comparison for the normal workflow. It allows different copy and content-driven widths while checking measured styling. Evidence can point to a concrete discrepancy, such as an observed font size and the expected value, instead of leaving the reviewer with an unexplained red result.

Saved screenshots also have limits. An uploaded image is a reference, not a freshly executed test. A recorded check describes the capture that produced it, not every subsequent revision of the website. Keeping those distinctions visible makes the result easier to trust.

Where this fits into CI/CD

Continuous integration checks whether a change can join the shared codebase safely. Continuous delivery prepares a reviewed change for release. Visual evidence adds another question to that process: does the interface still look and behave as intended?

My working review procedure is to update the component, inspect it in Storybook, capture the equivalent website example, compare the available references and resolve or explain the differences before publishing. The dashboard provides a place to retain that evidence and revisit the source.

The repository already has a Storybook workflow that performs lint checks and builds and publishes Storybook on its configured release path. That is separate from a visual regression gate. Automatic ingestion of dashboard results into CI, automatic Figma exports and broader browser coverage are still work ahead. This project documents the foundation and the current manual review step, rather than presenting a fully automated visual approval pipeline.

Private capture tools, public evidence

The editing workflow runs locally, where the dashboard server can launch a browser, save configuration and capture components. The public subdomain is a static export designed for ordinary shared hosting. It does not need a browser automation service running on the production server.

The export preserves recorded screenshots, uploaded reference PNGs, source links and the available embedded previews. Visitors can inspect the work, while editing, uploading and capture actions are disabled for public use. Changes made locally become public when I export and deploy a new snapshot.

This separation lets the portfolio show the process without giving visitors access to the configuration that produces the evidence. It also keeps the public site practical to host.

Making the procedure easier to use

The interface evolved around the act of comparing. Previews come first, settings sit with their source and secondary controls live behind the corresponding gear button. Shared Storybook buttons and icons keep the dashboard connected to the component system it reviews.

I reduced controls that distracted from that task: a separate combination table, unused comparison options and capture actions that implied broader state coverage than the normal workflow needed. The aim is to make it clear what is being compared and what a change will trigger.

The next step is to turn selected, reliable comparison cases into repeatable release checks, with explicit references and a review process for intentional design changes. Until then, the public dashboard is a transparent record of the available evidence and a practical workspace for developing that procedure.
